overview.body:
The technical design for Plans and Tasks, and how the work is divided. The Tasks under this Plan show how far it has come.

## What we are building

[A Plan stands on its own and reaches stories through its Tasks](annotation:model). It describes a body of work and how it can be executed in parallel. It is where the technical design for a change is drafted, and its Tasks are how the work gets done. It sits in its own section: Documentation is what is, Plans is what we will do, Reviews is what we did.

## Records

```text
change.saga/___plans/<plan-id>.plan/
  plan.json              id, title, phases, prototypes, reviews, delivered_at
  deck/                  a flat deck bundle, role plan, as a review's deck is
  tasks/<task-id>.task/
    task.json            title, phase, story, depends_on, code, sizing, state, summary
    essay.md             optional
```

Each choice serves one rule:

- **Git is the history.** `plan.json` and `task.json` have no revisions or event graphs, and changing them is committing them again. The Plan's slides keep the revision record any deck's slides keep.
- **One file per Task,** so agents on parallel branches marking different Tasks done touch different files.
- **`depends_on` is stored and `unblocks` is derived.** Adding a Task then edits only that Task, unless `--unblocks` also edits the Tasks it unblocks.
- **Plan and Task commands take no request IDs.** Retries are still safe: adding an existing id is refused, and writing the same state again changes nothing. Slide requests carry a `request_id`, as on any deck.

`internal/saga/plan.go` holds the model, `internal/planstore/planstore.go` the writes, `internal/cli/plans.go` the commands, and `internal/server/plans.go` the pages.

## Every Task leads to a story

[A Task names a user story or unblocks a Task that leads to one](annotation:chain), refactors included. There has to be a story somewhere, otherwise what are we doing? That also gives a clear chain of dependencies: a refactor with no story of its own shows exactly which story it serves.

`PlanTaskProblems` checks this in one walk: start from every Task that names a story, and walk backwards through `depends_on`. Any Task not reached is refused. Each Task and dependency is visited once, so every write can afford the check, and `validate` runs the same check over every Plan. A write that would strand a Task or make a cycle is refused and names the Tasks. Tasks are added top-down: the Task with the story first, then `task add --unblocks` for its prerequisites.

The sizing goal is being confident each Task would have taken two days or less before AI, which implies it is well understood.

## The deck

[The deck holds the technical design and shows how far the work has come](annotation:deck). A Plan's deck reuses the review deck's path in a new `plan` role that owes no code evidence. Slide sections group slides, usually by phase. An Item's `record` names a Task, and done state is read when the page opens, so nobody republishes a slide to report progress. Done is what an agent reports; it never proves the work is correct.

## Reading a Plan

[A Plan reads as an essay and a deck, beside a board of its Tasks](annotation:views). It opens on this essay, in the viewer a review's deck uses. Deck and Tasks sit in the header, and each is its own page. A slide's button opens its Tasks in a slide-out.

A phase is a set of Tasks that can run in parallel, and the next phase follows it, so a Task can only depend on Tasks of an earlier phase. A write that breaks this is refused. Phases keep their names because a slide section can use them.

Tasks is a whiteboard, drawn from the records so nobody authors it: a column per phase, ending at a column of stories. Selecting a node marks the path to it and shows where it leads. A Task shows its detail, and a story shows every Task it takes. A Task's own page draws only its chain, with the Task selected. Stories by feature and the Plan vs Reviews comparison sit above the board, and prototypes are linked beside the deck.

## Reviews and delivery

[A Plan and its Reviews reference each other](annotation:reviews), and share one Git history, so checking out a Review gives the Plan as it stood. A review Item naming a Task says it delivers that Task, and a callout naming one says why the work departed. The comparison reads those links. It only reports: it never blocks a merge, and a person still judges whether the work matches.

`plan deliver` is explicit, and is refused until every Task is done, at least one Review is linked, and every linked Review has merged. A delivered Plan is hidden as a merged review is, still reads, and no longer changes.

## The guide

[`plan guide` gives an agent the workflow](annotation:guide): research, ask, draft, prototype, size, explain, check. With `--plan` it names the Tasks not yet confidently two days or less, and what the deck still needs. The skill tells agents to author Saga content near completion, so a Plan has its own route there.

## Removing the old work plan

[The old work plan goes, so there is one way to plan work](annotation:old). It was the same idea, built earlier: a work item is what a Task is, and a wave is what a Phase is. An audit found it connected and unused: no records of it in this repository, no reader page, and `RecordContractState` and `ReviseContract` had no callers outside tests, so a dependency on a contract could never be satisfied through a public command. No Saga outside this repository uses it.

This gives something up. `plan record-merge` was the only path from a criterion to a merge commit, though nothing used it. Tasks also work differently from stories and terms, which keep revisions and event graphs. Contracts and workspace assignment return only if parallel agents turn out to need them.

Readiness's plan coverage now counts criteria whose story a Task names. Its delivery coverage was already separate: it counts a `verifies` relation from a claim or verification, and ignores test cases, so this repository reads 0 of 29. That is a separate question and is not changed here.

## Risks and open questions

- **Stale code references on Tasks.** They are pinned at the commit they were written, and nothing reports them as stale yet.
- **Approvals.** A Plan has no per-slide decisions or comments in this version. The deck format would allow adding them.
- **How far an agent can change a Plan.** Marking Tasks done is clear. Adding Tasks or rewriting slides is allowed by the commands, and whether it should be is untested.
